US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”
Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.
In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.
‘We’ve been preparing for the worst all year’: uncertainty grips Iran after Trump midterms defeat
The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday , when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.
The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.
In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.
Donald Trump speaks to reporters on arrival at Palm Beach, Florida. Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.
US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.
Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.
“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.
A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.
US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.
The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.
The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

items.title: Trump says U.S. carried out ‘minor strikes’ on Iran as missiles hit Qeshm Island
items.summary: Trump said the U.S. carried out ‘minor strikes’ on Iran after Iranian media reported two missiles hit Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz.
items.content:
Trump says U.S. carried out ‘minor strikes’ on Iran
President Donald Trump said the U.S. carried out “minor strikes” on Iran after reports that two missiles struck Qeshm Island.
Trump did not explicitly confirm that the U.S. strikes he described were the reported strikes on Qeshm Island.
The U.S. also struck Qeshm Island on Monday, in what a U.S. official described as a “defensive measure.”
WEST PALM BEACH, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 06: U.S President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after arriving on Air Force One at President Donald J. Trump International Airport on November 06, 2026 in West Palm Beach, Florida. Trump spoke at the UP.Summit, part of a multi-day technology expo and air show hosted by NASA showcasing American air and space innovation, earlier today. (Photo by Samuel Corum/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump told reporters Friday that the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" on Iran, amid reports that two missiles struck Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz.
The missiles struck the island on Friday, Iranian news agency Tasnim reported, according to Reuters . Tasnim said there was no official information on damage, Reuters added.
The island lies off Iran's southern coast, near the Strait of Hormuz, the vital artery for oil and gas that has become a flashpoint in the war.
Speaking to reporters Friday evening after landing in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump didn't comment specifically on Qeshm Island, saying: "I don't want to talk about it."
But he added: "We do minor strikes, but they knock out. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five." He did not explicitly confirm that he was referring to the reported strikes on Qeshm.
The strikes are the first since Tuesday's midterm elections, after analysts and regional officials had debated whether the vote would lead Trump toward further escalation or renewed diplomacy.
The U.S. struck the same island Monday, in what a U.S. official told MS Now was a " defensive measure ."
Trump also told reporters Friday that Iran wants "to make a deal very badly. They have 300% inflation. Their navy's gone. Their airport, everything's gone, and they want to make a deal."
The International Monetary Fund forecast that Iran's consumer prices would rise by an average of 78.6% in 2026, in a report published Oct. 13.
When asked if he wanted to make a deal "really soon," Trump said: "Well, we have nobody getting hurt, nobody getting killed.
"You know, this is a war that we may have been there for seven months, but we probably fought for three or four weeks, really fought. And again, you look at World War One; that's a war. World War Two; that's a war."
Iran has said it wants more than "paper commitments" from the U.S. before entering a new phase of diplomatic talks.
"We must see practical measures by the Americans," Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state broadcaster IRIB on Friday, according to Press TV .

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say 2 oil tankers hit mines, caught fire near Strait of Hormuz
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say 2 oil tankers hit mines, caught fire near Strait of Hormuz
IRGC says vessels switched off navigation systems, attempted passage through unauthorized route
ISTANBUL Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said late Saturday that two oil tankers were burning after striking naval mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the tankers switched off their navigation and positioning systems and attempted to use an unauthorized route. It accused both vessels of multiple violations, saying one was hit east of the strait and the other inside it.
Earlier on Saturday, the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) said an American aircraft disabled a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman after repeated attempts to breach the US naval blockade of Iran. CENTCOM identified the vessel as the St. Kitts-flagged Huda and said it had visited an Iranian port.
Tensions over navigation in the strait have continued since the US and Israeli offensive against Iran that began in late February and has yet to be settled.

Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Under the Qatari proposal, Iran would open the waterway on the second day of the deal being implemented. Photograph: Reuters
Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Under the Qatari proposal, Iran would open the waterway on the second day of the deal being implemented. Photograph: Reuters
Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of Qatari plan for Iran nuclear inspections
Trump still considering new assault on Iran nuclear sites – though threats less credible after Vance remarks
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.
The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.
Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms .
Midterms: how the blue wave took Congress, in three minutes – video
Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.
Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.
In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.
Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.
A billboard bearing the message ‘we will kill Trump’ in Tehran. Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.
In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.
Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.
Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.
The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.
It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.
The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.
The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

items.title: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections - CNBC
items.summary: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections  CNBC
items.content:
Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic election sweep
Crude oil prices sold off this week as investors hoped the Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections would force an end to the Iran war.
But tensions remain high in the Middle East, with the Gulf states still bracing for escalation, analysts say.
The Democrats' options are limited until they take control of Congress in January.
And President Donald Trump has reiterated that he will not allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.
80% odds of renewed military attack in Iran, oil risk premium to head higher
The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats' decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say.
Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans' stinging loss on the war. Vance's remarks raised questions about whether the administration still has support to continue the conflict with Iran.
The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren't sworn in until January, the analysts say.
"Throughout the week, we were struck by the divergence between deepening escalation concerns in the Gulf and the headline-driven off-ramp optimism of market participants thousands of miles away," Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told investors in a note Friday.
Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after the tanker ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, according to media reports. Iran state media also reported on explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several blasts occurring in the port of Jask. CNBC couldn't independently confirm the reports.
Several oil tankers have also come under attack near Oman since the election, killing one seafarer, according to maritime security agencies. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen continue to fire missiles at neighboring Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military buildup continues, with a third carrier strike group en route to the region. The consulting group Rapidan Energy sees an 80% chance that fighting will resume as diplomacy stalls.
Trump told reporters Thursday that he will make a decision soon on whether to attack Iran again.
"I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible but maybe I'll have to," Trump said in the Oval Office. "You'll know soon enough."
"We're locked and loaded," the president said. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in."
'Very good chance' we go back to conflict in Iran, says fmr. WH senior advisor Amos Hochstein
Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, traded above $97 on Friday, while U.S. crude was around $90.
"President Donald Trump is determined as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Friday.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it," the analyst said. The escalation dynamic remains in place so long as that core difference between the U.S. and Iran persists, he said.
The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump no longer faces future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden . Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC's " Power Lunch " Friday.
Tehran has been taunting the Trump administration since the election. The social media account of Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the "process of the U.S.'s collapse has accelerated" after the midterm results.
And Congress is unlikely to pass a war powers resolution until Democrats take control in January. Trump can veto such a resolution anyway.
The main leverage Congress will have is the power of the purse, Croft said. Government funding expires on Dec. 11, and negotiations for another continuing resolution could drag into 2027, she said. This would give Democrats more leverage when they take power in January, the analyst said.
"Importantly, deferring funding decisions would not immediately constrain Trump's ability to conduct military operations, but could significantly reshape the administration's longer-term funding outlook," Croft told investors.
Trump discussed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region with the emir of Qatar during a Friday phone call, according to Qatar's state news agency .
An unnamed senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar. Tehran will only discuss the proposal after the U.S. meets its demands, the Iranian official told Reuters.
Trump seemed to dismiss the diplomatic efforts Thursday.
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the president said. "They're not doing anything without our approval. It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," he said of the diplomatic efforts.

Tehran, Iran – The United States has bombed Iran after vessels were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators continue to try to prevent large-scale fighting between the two countries.
Two projectiles hit Iran’s Qeshm on Friday night, the latest in a series of air strikes on the southern island over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defences and launchers. President Donald Trump called them “minor strikes” , amid increasing concerns of a potential escalation in the war between the countries.

list 2 of 3 Will Trump strike nuclear sites again as Iran engages ‘cognitive warfare’?
list 3 of 3 Qatari PM says US willing to seek solution to war with Iran
Iran’s army said in the early hours of Saturday that it destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone using an unnamed new system. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) separately claimed on Friday that its air defences intercepted an MQ-1, reportedly the 16th aircraft of this model to be destroyed since the start of the war.
At least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the week ending on November 6, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which said three of them sank. The Western military intelligence agency has recorded 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in early July, although it has cautioned that most attacks are going unreported .
UKMTO’s weekly report also identified 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits in the Strait of Hormuz, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Most of the vessels that travel with their transponders switched on are using the Iranian route to the north. But many ships are still attempting the southern route near Oman with their tracking systems offline to shuttle oil out of the waterway .
Iranian armed forces also claim that, in addition to being hit with missiles and drones, tankers and commercial vessels using “unauthorised” routes also run the risk of being hit by naval mines.
The Iranian military’s naval force said on Saturday that a tanker with its transponder turned off caught fire in the eastern area of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine. Washington says the mines have been cleared.
For years, the IRGC maintained that it was limiting the range of its ballistic missiles to about 2,000 kilometres (1,240 miles) to reassure European countries that they would not be targeted.
But with Trump threatening to resume extensive air strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure, commanders say nothing is off limits now.
“This limitation has been lifted for us,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told reporters during an event on Saturday, in reference to missile range constraints.
His comments came after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an unrestrained military response to any future threats from Israel and the US. Iran’s aerospace division of the IRGC has prepared “surprising defence achievements” that will be deployed in action if another wave of major attacks starts, he added.
“The operational unveiling of these [advanced] achievements in case of new conflict will not only frustrate and fascinate enemies, but will further solidify Iran’s military authority on the global stage, make the resistance front happy, and fully neutralise aggressors’ calculations,” Mohebbi said.
The spokesman said the IRGC plans to unveil another underground “missile city” soon, and will deploy some combat systems to public spaces so the people can personally inspect them.
Mohebbi added that if the Islamic republic decides to alter its nuclear doctrine and build a bomb, the necessary preparations will be made.
On state television’s war-focused Be Vaght-e Iran (At Iran’s Time) programme over the weekend, presenters and analysts said Iranian armed forces had their fingers on the trigger and were especially eyeing any movement from Israel.
“Our military information about the strategic chokepoints of Israel is complete. If our water, electricity and natural gas is cut off, they will also be plunged into darkness and lack of water,” one analyst said. “This is not a bluff, but a serious warning.”
Over recent weeks, diplomatic efforts by mediators to avoid attacks that could damage the entire region have picked up, although with limited gains.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he held talks with 12 foreign ministers over the past 48 hours, including top diplomats from Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
He said he explained the “fundamental positions” of Tehran, including the seven demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and stressed the need to form “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.
Security chief Mohsen Rezaei reportedly emphasised the same conditions to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a visit to Moscow on Thursday, which was also aimed at delivering a message from Khamenei.
Pro-Israel hawk Stephen Miller has been appointed as chief of staff by President Donald Trump [Win McNamee/Getty Images] Developments between Iran and the US resemble a “constant pendulum swing between war and negotiations” that is increasingly leaning towards conflict, according to political analyst Mostafa Najafi, who is said to be close to Iran’s security chief.
“What is clear for now is that the movement of this pendulum will continue; a conflict whose ending is much more complicated and time-consuming than imagined,” he wrote on X. The historic defeat for Trump and the Republicans in US midterm elections this week may further complicate the picture, he added.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said three factors increase the risk of war in the short term after the elections, unless negotiations lead to a breakthrough.
The political cost of high fuel prices, brought about largely due to the war on Iran, has already been paid, he said, and there won’t be another point on the political calendar soon for Trump to worry about this issue.
“On the one hand, the pressure to get a deal will dissipate,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pressure from pro-war hawks will also escalate significantly because they will be constrained in their efforts to step up the conflict after the Democrats take control of Congress in early January. The appointment of far-right, pro-Israel hawk Stephen Miller as chief of staff also hints that Trump might not be ready to wind down the war.
“Finally, there is a new psychological element to Trump’s mindset following this humiliation: Trump’s desire for vengeance. There has been a vindictive element to his calculations in the past weeks because of his anger over how Iran – in Trump’s mind – has ruined his presidency,” Parsi said.

items.title: Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
items.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
items.content:
Image caption, Employees inspect the damage of a kindergarten in Kyiv following a Russian missile attack
By Olivia Ireland Â  and Â  Dan Johnson ,Â  Reporting from in Kyiv
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram , external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Image caption, Debris and a broken window inside the kindergarten in Kyiv
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire , which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia , with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.

Egypt Eyes Billions in New Investment to Revive Oil and Gas Production
Egypt aims to raise natural gas production to 6.6 billion cubic feet per day by 2027 through increased drilling and foreign investment.
Eni is expanding operations with plans for 230 wells, while its recent offshore gas discovery could accelerate production growth.
Egypt has settled $6.1 billion in overdue payments to energy partners and is modernizing infrastructure to encourage investment.
The Egyptian government is doubling down on its plans to accelerate the development of its oil and gas resources. Egypt now aims to achieve a production capacity of 6.6 billion cubic feet per day by 2027, s upported by increased drilling, new exploration incentives, and greater investment from international oil and gas majors.
In October, the Egyptian Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, Karim Badawi, met with Cypriot Energy Minister Michael Damianos, East Mediterranean Gas Forum Secretary-General Osama Mobarez and international oil and gas executives from firms operating in Egypt during the “The Future of Energy in Egypt” roundtable to discuss how the country might accelerate investment in the sector and boost production.
The government aims to speed up the development of discoveries and connect them to the country’s existing infrastructure to maximise economic returns from the sector. Badawi said that the ministry hopes to strengthen regional cooperation and establish Egypt as a regional hub. The government plans to address development challenges in partnership with international partners to create the necessary conditions to encourage further investment in the sector.
In recent years, oil and gas production has fallen, largely due to ageing Mediterranean offshore fields, particularly the giant Zohr gas field. The country is seeking greater investment in developing oil and gas discoveries, thereby reducing reliance on mature operations. Egypt hopes to continue using existing infrastructure to reduce the cost of new operations and encourage greater investment in the sector. Egypt is home to vast transportation networks, gas reception, and trading facilities. It has liquefaction capabilities and is strategically located with access to various markets.
During the opening ceremony of the Mediterranean Oil and Gas Conference and Exhibition in October, Badawi said   that Egypt had brought 591 new wells into production and made 113 discoveries between July 2024 and June 2026. The minister said that Egypt had been able to attract higher levels of investment, having successfully paid the outstanding debts that it owed to investment partners in exploration, discovery, and production activities.
Earlier in the year, President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi announced plans to double crude oil and condensate production as part of a five-year energy strategy during a meeting with Badawi. The government also plans to invest over $4 billion to improve six refineries by modernising existing refineries, raising domestic production of higher-value petroleum products, and reducing Egypt’s fuel import bill.
The five-year strategy focuses on seismic surveys, advanced technologies, new contractual frameworks, and the development of discoveries that have yet to enter production. Al-Sisi has encouraged the government to offer additional incentives to international partners to attract more investment in the sector and encourage new exploration projects.
Al-Sisi also met with the CEO of the Italian oil and gas major Eni, Claudio Descalzi, to discuss expansion. Descalzi stated plans to increase its investment in Egypt, with plans to drill 30 exploration wells and 200 development wells. Eni has invested around $8.5 billion in Egypt to date, producing approximately 242,000 bpd of oil equivalent in 2025 through its subsidiary International Egyptian Oil Company.
Eni aims to increase its production in Egypt by developing new discoveries and leveraging the country’s existing infrastructure to accelerate deployment. Connecting existing infrastructure to new developments will help reduce the time required to advance new projects and extend the operating life of fields already in production. Eni will expand operations in various parts of the country, including the Mediterranean, the Nile Delta, Sinai, and the Western Desert.
The company has already begun using these initiatives and has reported a 50 per cent increase in output from its offshore fields in Sinai. In April, Eni made a significant gas and condensate discovery in the Temsah Concession, located offshore in the Eastern Mediterranean, with preliminary estimates indicating 2 trillion cubic feet of gas and 130 million barrels of associated condensate. The discovery is less than 10 km from existing infrastructure, making it easier to quickly establish connectivity. In August, Eni said that first gas from the discovery would be achieved in less than two years.
In October, Eni announced plans to increase its gas processing capacity in Egypt’s Western Desert through phase two of its Meleiha project in the Merged Meleiha concession. The new facility is expected to process up to 100 million standard cubic feet of gas per day once operational, supporting the government’s aims to accelerate the rollout of new gas production capacity. This will increase the availability of gas for the domestic market, according to the company.
Having settled old debts, Egypt now hopes to encourage greater investment in oil and gas exploration and development over the coming years to help reverse the declining output seen in recent years. Eni has already committed to increasing investment in the North African country and will use Egypt’s existing infrastructure to bring new production online quickly.

Goldman Sachs Cuts Gold Price Forecasts as Hawkish Federal Reserve Weighs on Demand
Gold bar and coins ©Adobe Stock Images Goldman Sachs has lowered its gold price forecasts for the end of 2026 and 2027, citing the Federal Reserve's increasingly hawkish monetary policy stance and its impact on investor demand. However, the investment bank maintained a positive longer-term outlook, supported by substantial central bank purchases.
Strategists led by Lina Thomas reduced their end-2026 gold price target to $4,150 per ounce from $4,650. The forecast for the end of 2027 was lowered to $4,800 per ounce from $5,400.
The revised projections assume that the Fed's tighter policy stance, including an anticipated interest rate increase in December, will limit demand for gold as protection against currency depreciation and broader economic policy risks.
Goldman expects investor demand for gold as a hedge against monetary and fiscal uncertainty to return toward historical averages rather than revisit the elevated levels recorded earlier in 2026.
The bank compared current market conditions with 2022, when strong central bank purchases supported gold prices but higher interest rates limited investment demand.
Higher borrowing costs generally reduce the attractiveness of gold because the precious metal does not generate interest income.
Goldman also expects demand for gold call options, which can reflect investor interest in protection against policy-related risks, to moderate.
Despite reducing its near-term forecasts, Goldman continues to view central bank demand as a significant structural driver of gold prices.
The bank expects central banks to purchase approximately 60 tonnes of gold per month throughout 2026 and 2027, substantially above the average of 17 tonnes recorded before 2022.
Its latest estimate places current purchases at approximately 85 tonnes per month, based on a seasonally adjusted three-month average.
"We retain our longer-term constructive view on structurally strong central bank demand – which drives most of the 15% price upside we forecast by end-2027," the strategists wrote.
Goldman noted that emerging-market central banks, particularly China, continue to hold relatively low gold allocations compared with potential long-term reserve targets.
Developed-market central banks have generally participated less in the recent purchasing trend, partly because they already maintain substantial historical gold reserves.
"But the debate is increasingly shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, pointing to broader concerns around reserve security and cross-country trust," the strategists added.
Goldman expects gold prices to receive additional support when the Federal Reserve begins reducing interest rates.
The bank's economists anticipate rate cuts beginning in late 2027 and continuing into early 2028, potentially easing pressure on gold and encouraging renewed private investment demand.
For shorter-term investors, however, the outlook remains challenging.
Goldman identified rising interest rates, uncertain energy prices and restrictive risk limits as potential obstacles for commodity trading advisers and macro hedge funds over the next three to six months.
Higher oil prices could also trigger additional selling by systematic investment strategies.
The bank warned that gold could face further downward pressure if the Fed raises rates again in March 2027, delays monetary easing or increases its projected terminal interest rate.
Under that scenario, Goldman estimates gold could reach $4,660 per ounce by the end of 2027, below its revised base-case forecast of $4,800.
Conversely, renewed concerns about government debt sustainability and fiscal policy could increase demand for gold as a hedge, potentially pushing prices above the bank's central forecast.
Goldman suggested that longer-term investors seeking exposure to sustained central bank purchases or protection against economic policy risks may view the current correction as a potential entry opportunity.

Ukraine war briefing: Beijing confirms historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting under discussion
Russia could use tri leader summit to nudge China and US closer to its position on Ukraine, experts say. What we know on day 1,718
Beijing has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the US president, Donald Trump, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin . Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state”, which could take place on the sidelines of the Apec summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen this month.
Russia would probably use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow’s positions on Ukraine , said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. However, Trump has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Danny Russel, a former senior state department official who served in Barack Obama’s administration and who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
Ukraine again came under attack from Russia on Saturday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated his calls for allies to supply Kyiv quickly with missiles for the US-made Patriot system to defend Ukrainian cities . Zelenskyy on Friday had warned that the Ukrainian military was bracing for new ⁠strikes ​by Russian forces against important infrastructure. “We ⁠have intelligence at this time that Russia is preparing new strikes on energy, on ⁠bridges across the Dnipro, on civilian infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said ​in his nightly ‌video address. “The ‌air force and the armed forces of Ukraine ‌as a whole are preparing for defence. It will not be easy.”
Kyiv, along with other Ukrainian cities, has been subjected to near-constant attacks for several weeks. A missile attack by Russian forces ⁠early on Saturday damaged a residential ⁠building in the Ukrainian capital , according to Mayor ​Vitali ‌Klitschko. The city’s military administration, also writing on Telegram, said two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was ‌damaged. Russian attacks also damaged energy facilities in the Kyiv region affecting operation of heating and water supply systems in the city, while an important bridge was also hit, Klitschko said, adding “the capital’s energy supply is extremely difficult”. Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours ​after the attack.
President Zelenskyy says he wants specific guarantees from western allies on how postwar security support would function when the war with Russia finally ends . Zelenskyy’s comments in an interview aired late Thursday followed two days of discussions among allies in Brussels that focused on postwar security and reconstruction. They also came before planned three-way talks next week in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the United States, the first trilateral peace discussions since February. “What matters is that it’s clear on paper,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukraine’s private 1+1 television broadcast late Thursday. “The question isn’t dozens of points, but simply an understanding of the outcome: If Russia starts [attacking] again, what will happen? Who will do what, with what means, and when?”
The Brussels meetings brought together officials from the US, UK, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock , Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post. “We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them,” Umerov wrote.

items.title: Trump stands by Hegseth as GOP criticism mounts and he pushes to restart the Iran war - Yahoo
items.summary: Trump stands by Hegseth as GOP criticism mounts and he pushes to restart the Iran war  Yahoo</f
items.content:
President Trump looks on as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks in Doral, Fla., in March. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran following the historic drubbing Republicans took from Democrats in this week's midterm elections. But President Trump has said he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet.
"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters. On Thursday, Trump said Hegseth had "done a fantastic job," Reuters reported .
The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor this week.
"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat.
According to CBS News , though, Trump "has been asking advisers" whether Hegseth should stay or go. The White House has denied reports that Hegseth would leave his job in a post-election shake-up, the BBC reported . The Pentagon has said Hegseth is "100 percent committed" to serving through the end of Trump's term.
Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices.
Hegseth has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing U.S. officials. Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict, the Journal reported.
Hegseth leaves a meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines on Oct. 28.
Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal.
"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war."
The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did.
Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning."
"He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress."
Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him.
"I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it."
Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Friday that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."
"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer told NewsNation .
The U.S. Capitol building is seen in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4.
When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list.
"In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month .
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky and vocal Trump critic, said he intends to force a House vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as next week, citing violations of the War Powers Resolution, bypassing Congress on war declarations and unlawful military actions in several countries.
Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the Republican primary — introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote.
In a post on X Wednesday , Massie wrote that "there is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns."
A fire burns at an oil depot in Tehran, Iran, on March 8 after U.S. and Israeli attacks.
In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Thursday afternoon, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit.
"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me."
Tillis responded on X. "Cabinet secretaries shouldn't be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos," he wrote, adding that the issue was "the incompetence you've displayed" and "the bad advice you've given to president."

items.title: Grand Theft Hardware As Thieves Steal $11.4M NVIDIA Chip Shipment - HotHardware
items.summary: Grand Theft Hardware As Thieves Steal $11.4M NVIDIA Chip Shipment  HotHardware
items.content:
Grand Theft Hardware As Thieves Steal $11.4M NVIDIA Chip Shipment
Thieves stole pallets of NVIDIA hardware - Image: Alexas_Fotos via Pixabay (edited with ChatGPT)
As the cost of GPUs, memory, and storage keeps going up , PC enthusiasts could be forgiven for calling the current hardware market highway robbery. But in California, the expression took a more literal turn after thieves made off with half a dozen pallets of NVIDIA hardware worth an estimated $11.4 million.
The details sound like a mission you might come across in Grand Theft Auto VI , except this actually happened in real life, and not in Florida. According to ABC7 News , citing reporting by the Bay Area News Group, the shipment departed Oakland, California, on August 29 and was destined for Fort Worth, Texas. Somewhere along the line, the shipment disappeared.
A truck disguised as a food transportation vehicle picked up the pallets of NVIDIA chips "as planned," but something went wrong after it left Oakland. Investigators attempting to retrace its movements eventually lost track of the truck and its drivers in San Bernardino County. The outlet's reporting is confusingly worded, so it's not clear if the shipper intentionally used a supposed food truck to avoid being targeted by thieves only to still get hijacked, or if the thieves used a vehicle disguised as a food truck to gain entry to the facility and then steal the pallets of hardware. Either way, the goods are gone.
In a statement, the Oakland Police Department confirmed that it received a grand theft report on September 13, more than two weeks after the original pickup. The investigation remains ongoing, and authorities have not yet announced any arrests.
It's unclear exactly which NVIDIA products were inside the shipment. Given the company's extensive lineup of AI accelerators, server equipment, and consumer GPUs, there are numerous possibilities. Authorities also haven't disclosed how the cargo disappeared or whether any of the stolen equipment has been recovered.
Whatever was stolen, thieves could potentially fetch way over face value if the hot goods find their way overseas. Speaking to the outlet, Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business, said thieves have "lots and lots of incentives to hijack those chips anywhere where security is weak."
"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," Groth added.
This also isn't the first NVIDIA-related theft to make headlines in the Bay Area. Last year, police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA cargo. And in another brazen heist, thieves made off with a truckload of Apple products and AMD chips worth $15 million in Nevada last year.
Then there was the rather amusing September incident we covered previously , when thieves apparently thought they'd struck GPU gold by stealing two NVIDIA-branded trailers. Instead, they wound up with 40,000 pounds of sand being used as ballast for autonomous truck testing. Yes, to lean into another expression, thieves who thought they hit pay dirt ended up pounding sand instead.
The latest reported incident is far more serious, with an eight-figure shipment still unaccounted for. According to Groth, incidents like this are a "national security concern" because the stolen goods could end up in a region where exports of AI chips are banned or "anywhere we have conflict in the area." Whether investigators can recover the hardware remains to be seen.
Paul is a seasoned geek who cut this teeth on the Commodore 64. When he's not geeking out to tech, he's out riding his Harley and collecting stray cats.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of Qatari plan for Iran nuclear inspections - The Guardian
items.summary: Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of Qatari plan for Iran nuclear inspections  The Guardian
items.content:
Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Under the Qatari proposal, Iran would open the waterway on the second day of the deal being implemented. Photograph: Reuters
Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Under the Qatari proposal, Iran would open the waterway on the second day of the deal being implemented. Photograph: Reuters
Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of Qatari plan for Iran nuclear inspections
Trump still considering new assault on Iran nuclear sites – though threats less credible after Vance remarks
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.
The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.
Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms .
Midterms: how the blue wave took Congress, in three minutes – video
Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.
Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.
In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.
Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.
A billboard bearing the message ‘we will kill Trump’ in Tehran. Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.
In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.
Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.
Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.
The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.
It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.
The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.
The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

items.title: President Donald Trump Just Proclaimed That "Inflation Is Way Down," but Federal Reserve Economists Have a Different Take - The Motley Fool
items.summary: President Donald Trump Just Proclaimed That "Inflation Is Way Down," but Federal Reserve Economists Have a Different Take  <font color="#6f6f
items.content:
Statistically, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have excelled under Donald Trump.
The president has repeatedly called on the central bank to slash interest rates.
A recent study by New York Fed economists found that Trump’s tariffs have increased goods prices.
Persistently elevated inflation presents challenges for a historically expensive, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven bull market that can ill afford any hiccups.
From a purely statistical standpoint, Wall Street has relished having Donald Trump in the White House. The average annual return of the timeless Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI -0.46% ) , benchmark S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.31% ) , and tech-driven Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +1.09% ) is decisively higher under Trump than under most other presidents over the last 130 years.
There's little question that the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and the ongoing AI infrastructure build-out have been paramount to this outperformance in President Trump's nonconsecutive second term. The president's favorable tax policy -- the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanently lowered the peak marginal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21% -- has played an important role, too.
President Trump's policies are contributing factors to elevated inflation. Image source: Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok.
But things may not be as picture-perfect for Wall Street as the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite suggest. Though the stock market has made a habit of climbing the proverbial wall of worry for years, eventually stocks will stumble.
Perhaps no stock market headwind is greater at the moment than persistently elevated inflation. While President Trump has been adamant that "inflation is way down" under his administration , Federal Reserve economists have a different take.
President Trump has repeatedly criticized the Fed for not lowering interest rates
Despite the Consumer Price Index reaching a three-year high of 4.2% in May, Trump has been firm in his stance that prices are rising at a much tamer pace under his administration than under his predecessor.
In particular, the president has latched onto the strength of the job market -- the unemployment rate remains near historic lows -- and the stated temporary nature of the Iran war as reasons not to be concerned with inflation . Donald Trump has opined on several occasions that oil prices and, therefore, fuel prices, would plunge once the Iran war ends. This would, in his view, quickly remedy energy-commodity-driven inflation.
BREAKING: President Trump says inflation is “way down.”
“The golden age of America is upon us,” Trump says. https://t.co/AqW5HjnBDj
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) October 30, 2026
Modest inflation, or even the perception of moderating inflation, is foundational to President Trump's repeated calls for the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates.
Since the start of his second term on Jan. 20, 2025, Trump has been feuding almost nonstop with the central bank over interest rates . He criticized now-former Fed Chair Jerome Powell for the Fed's slow-stepped rate-easing cycle. While the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) lowered the federal funds target rate six times between September 2024 and December 2025 to 3.50%-3.75%, the president believes lending rates should be slashed to 1% (or lower).
Although the new Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh, has largely avoided these criticisms, the same can't be said about the other voting members of the FOMC.
President Trump wants to see interest rates head lower, because reduced borrowing costs would spur hiring and fuel the AI infrastructure build-out. Furthermore, interest rate cuts would make it considerably easier for the U.S. to service its more than $40 trillion in total debt .
Federal Reserve economists have bad news for Trump (and Wall Street): inflation is rising
However, inflation isn't "way down," as Donald Trump has proclaimed. Though annualized inflation is well below its four-decade high of 9.1% in June 2022, the reported annualized rate of 3.7% for September is nearly double the FOMC's long-term target of 2%.
Keep in mind that consumer prices are expected to rise when the U.S. economy is expanding. If businesses are firing on all cylinders, they should possess some degree of pricing power over their goods and services.
The issue is that annualized inflation has moved well above what Warsh and the FOMC would consider "modest," and two of the president's policies are mostly to blame.
New from the New York Fed: "By February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 pp to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly."
About one quarter of every point in higher tariff rates shows up in consumer prices within one year.
• A 10% across-the-board tariff yields a 2.6% rise in consumer goods prices after one year.
• About two thirds of the increase comes from pricier imports, which get passed through quickly.
• Another third comes from U.S. made goods, as producers face higher input costs and less import competition. This takes longer, about 6-12 months, to filter through.
Despite Trump's recent claim that tariffs don't cause inflation , three New York Federal Reserve economists writing for Liberty Street Economics examined the inflationary effects of the president's 2025 tariffs on consumer prices. In their report ("How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?"), the authors estimated that Trump's tariffs raised goods price inflation by 2.9 percentage points by February 2026. Conversely, goods prices would have declined had Trump not imposed tariffs!
This isn't the first time that NY Fed economists at Liberty Street Economics have linked Trump's tariffs to higher prices, either. A December 2024 report ("Do Input Tariffs Protect U.S. Firms?") found that the president's 2018 China tariffs raised prices for select imported goods.
In addition to tariffs, the Trump-led Iran war has created the largest modern-day energy supply disruption. Even if a peace deal were hypothetically signed today, it would take months to restore energy production to normal in the region, and even longer to rebuild storage. The inflationary effects of the Iran war are here to stay for quite some time.
The AI boom is transforming one of the biggest deflationary forces into a key source of US inflation:
Import prices for computer and electronic products surged +7.4% in the first 6 months of 2026, to 77.1 points, the highest since January 2016.
This also marks a +8.0% YoY jump, the largest annual increase on record.
This represents a historic reversal from a downtrend which persisted for over two decades.
Between 2006 and 2019, computer and electronic product import prices fell -30%, as improving technology and manufacturing efficiency consistently pushed costs lower.
Now, the AI investment boom is straining manufacturing capacity for semiconductors, servers, and electronic components, as companies race to build out AI infrastructure regardless of cost.
The AI revolution has flipped technology from a long-term source of deflation into a major driver of inflation.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) July 21, 2026
The AI infrastructure build-out is also sparking inflation . The insatiable demand for AI data center hardware, coupled with persistent hardware supply shortages, has lifted prices all the way down to the consumer level. While President Trump's policies aren't responsible for AI-driven inflation, this is another data point that shows inflation isn't "way down."
Persistently elevated inflation is particularly worrisome for Wall Street. While banks and insurers can thrive amid a rate-hiking cycle, the same can't be said for high-growth tech stocks.
The AI build-out has been financed in part with debt. If borrowing costs continue to climb due to a confluence of factors, including the president's own policies, it threatens to slow this expansion. A historically expensive stock market can ill afford any hiccups . But with inflation remaining elevated and still climbing (as of September), the odds are growing of an aggressive rate-hiking cycle that ultimately wallops Wall Street.

Sean Williams is a data-driven Motley Fool contributing analyst who's been investing for 28 years and has penned north of 16,000 articles. You'll find him at the intersection of politics and investing tackling macroeconomic topics of interest (Social Security and Donald Trump's economic/tax policies), analyzing which stocks billionaire investors (e.g., Warren Buffett) are buying and selling, and digging into how the world's most-influential businesses and trends -- everything from the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) to the next stock split -- are changing Wall Street.
He holds a B.A. in Economics from the University of California, San Diego.

items.title: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I'd Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I'd Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Semiconductor stocks have dropped over the last month.
Foundry leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing already holds a massive market share in the chip manufacturing industry, and it could grow even larger in the years to come.
TSMC trades at a bargain level relative to its potential growth.
Investors have soured on AI stocks. The hyperscalers face pressure as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars annually on their AI build-outs, and several have already dipped into negative free-cash-flow territory. The neoclouds face significant financing challenges as their cost of capital continues to climb. And ultimately, that's all hitting the shares of the semiconductor companies that design and sell the chips that go into the data centers powering the proliferation of AI.
Semiconductor stocks as a class are down by about 30% since Oct. 6 (as measured by the benchmark PHLX Semiconductor Sector index). Few chip stocks have been spared. Nvidia ( NVDA +2.77% ) is down 21%, and Micron ( MU +5.12% ) is down 34%. Smart investors may see this pullback as an opportunity to buy chip stocks at a discount. Indeed, there are a growing number of attractive opportunities in the sector. But I wouldn't buy Nvidia or Micron stock at the current prices.
If I could buy and hold just one AI chip stock right now, it would be Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM +6.33% ) .
The company behind the most advanced chips in the world
Every company that's designing advanced chips for artificial intelligence relies heavily on TSMC to manufacture them. The world's largest third-party foundry has the most advanced chip production processes and the scale to meet the growing demand for advanced chips. As a result, its long-dominant market share has grown to 73% of contract semiconductor manufacturing spend.
TSMC benefits from a virtuous cycle that should ensure it maintains or even expands on that dominance. It generates huge revenues every quarter with a foundry operation that is significantly larger than all of its would-be rivals combined. That provides it with plenty of funds that it can reinvest in research and development to maintain its technological lead. It also provides more capital to invest in expanding its production capacity, enabling it to serve more customers and larger contracts. That, in turn, leads to additional revenue growth, restarting the cycle.
TSMC also benefits from its close working relationships with its largest customers, which help it identify opportunities for performance improvements and plan capital expenditures effectively to avoid overbuilding capacity. While the semiconductor industry is cyclical , TSMC's irreplaceable role in its customers' supply chains helps mitigate earnings volatility. By contrast, Micron and its fellow memory-chip makers continue to face valuation challenges due to the commodity-like nature of the chips they both design and manufacture.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $1.95T
To be sure, TSMC is investing significant capital to expand its production capacity. Management has guided for between $60 billion and $64 billion in capex spending this year, up from $40.9 billion in 2025 and $29.8 billion in 2024. Management expects to continue boosting its capex over the next two years.
But that spending should translate into strong revenue growth.
"The majority of the capex is always related to the long-term demand," CFO Wendell Huang said on the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We have no intention to leave any food on the table for others."
In other words, TSMC is using its dominant position today to ensure it remains the dominant force in contract semiconductor manufacturing for years to come, and to keep delivering strong revenue growth. Management's long-term guidance for 25% compound annualized revenue growth between 2024 and 2029 will need an update after the company grew sales 35.9% in 2025, and that number has accelerated in 2026.
After the recent sell-off in semiconductor stocks, TSMC shares now trade around 21 times forward earnings expectations. That's a similar level to Nvidia, but well above Micron's 4 multiple.
Micron's multiple is significantly lower due to the cyclical and commoditized nature of the memory chip industry . Pricing for memory chips has for decades been much more volatile than logic chips: How much Micron charges for its chips is dictated almost entirely by supply and demand conditions.
Despite a tight supply for the logic chips that TSMC manufactures, it hasn't hiked its prices by an exorbitant amount, and CEO C.C. Wei said TSMC will avoid sudden price hikes. That strategy, combined with its better supply and demand forecasting capabilities due to its position in the market, means TSMC's earnings are much more stable. Micron, by contrast, is expected to see its earnings start to drop in 2029 as more memory-chip manufacturing capacity comes online across the space and supply starts to catch up with demand.
While Nvidia is growing significantly faster than TSMC with much lower capital intensity, TSMC is the better long-term investment at the current price. It stands to benefit from the growing demand for semiconductors regardless of which companies are designing tomorrow's most popular data center chips. Its leading position in the industry is unlikely to change anytime soon. In other words, it's more predictable than Nvidia, which makes it a more attractive long-term opportunity.
With expectations for revenue growth well above 20% and TSMC's ability to maintain wide operating margins, the stock at its current earnings multiple looks like a bargain.

items.summary: Democrat shaping AI policy bought chip stocks despite backing congressional trading ban  CNBC
items.content:
Josh Gottheimer discloses AI stock buys after trading ban vote
Rep. Josh Gottheimer disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks, including Benchmark Electronics and Applied Materials, as he helps shape Democrats' AI agenda.
The New Jersey Democrat's trades came months after Gottheimer voted to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual stocks, a restriction he has supported for years.
There's no evidence of wrongdoing, but the investments face fresh scrutiny as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and ramp up oversight of the AI industry.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., speaks at a press conference at the Capitol in Washington, Jan. 27, 2023.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer , a Democrat helping write his party's artificial intelligence agenda, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks — just months after voting to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual shares.
The New Jersey Democrat disclosed an Oct. 12 purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 of Benchmark Electronics stock, according to a filing released this week. His jointly owned Morgan Stanley account also bought up to $15,000 worth of Applied Materials shares on Oct. 26, following three earlier purchases of leading AI chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices .
While there's no evidence of wrongdoing, the trades put Gottheimer's investments in the spotlight as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, gaining new power to regulate and investigate the AI industry.
Gottheimer, a former Microsoft executive, sits on the House Financial Services subcommittee overseeing AI in finance, has introduced legislation on AI regulations and co-chairs a commission developing Democrats' broader AI agenda.
Gottheimer's spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said the congressman turned over control of his investments to a third party with "full investment discretion" before taking office in 2017.
"Gottheimer is also awaiting approval from Congress of a blind trust. In the meantime, he has taken the extra step of setting up an independent trust," Bottomley said.
Democrats are already targeting the AI industry. Reps. Maxine Waters and Greg Casar introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts for AI companies, referred in part to Gottheimer's committee. Casar has also called for AI executives to testify under oath, while other Democrats are pushing to restrict data centers or halt new construction altogether.
The purchases also contrast with Gottheimer's longstanding support for restricting congressional stock trading . In July, he was among just 13 Democrats who voted for the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing most individual stocks. The bill passed the House but has not become law. Some Democrats opposed it both because it contained a voter-ID provision and because some said it should have gone further in curbing stock purchasing and holding by elected officials.
Four years earlier, Gottheimer backed legislation requiring lawmakers to place investments in blind trusts and pledged to establish one himself.
The AI purchases are just a small slice of Gottheimer's sprawling investment portfolio. The five trades totaled between $5,005 and $75,000, compared with $15.1 million to $59 million in disclosed household assets, including up to $44.5 million in stocks. His household has reported more than 1,100 securities transactions over three years, according to Follow the Filings . Gottheimer reports household assets jointly with his wife, Marla Tusk, who is general counsel at a political consulting firm.
Advanced Micro Devices competes with Nvidia in AI chips, while Applied Materials supplies semiconductor manufacturing equipment. It was also Benchmark's largest disclosed customer in 2025, accounting for 14% of revenue, according to a securities filing .
Benchmark, meanwhile, generated 30% of its third-quarter revenue from semiconductor equipment and another 16% from advanced computing and communications, according to its Oct. 28 earnings report . Gottheimer also disclosed an Applied Materials purchase in August and a sale in September.
The purchases came shortly before a sharp selloff in AI stocks. The Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.5% Thursday, as Nvidia dropped more than 9% and AMD roughly 17%. The index includes both companies.
Benchmark fell nearly 17% over Wednesday and Thursday, closing at $59.34 — roughly 25% below its closing price on Gottheimer's October purchase date — before recovering somewhat Friday.

items.summary:
