items.content:
About 600,000 of Nvidia's artificial intelligence (AI) chips are reportedly piled up in Hong Kong, unable to enter mainland China. The U.S. government allowed exports, but China has not approved large-scale imports.
China's big tech companies need high-performance U.S. chips to develop AI models, but the Chinese government is wary of rising dependence on U.S. technology. Policies aimed at protecting the domestic chip industry are instead becoming an obstacle for Chinese AI companies to secure chips.
On the 5th (local time), Reuters, citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported that about 600,000 of Nvidia's high-performance AI Semiconductor H200 chips are being stored in Hong Kong, unable to be brought into mainland China. This is the first time the specific quantity of H200s stacked in Hong Kong has been reported.
The Chinese government has in recent months allowed the entry of some H200s. Several major Chinese internet companies are each said to have secured about 10,000 H200s. Small quantities have also come in through brokers or indirect channels. However, authorities are still not approving large-scale imports.
◇ Need U.S. chips, but protecting domestic industry comes first
This situation stems from the overlap of U.S. export controls and China's chip self-sufficiency policy. Since 2022, the United States has restricted China's access to advanced AI Semiconductors and chipmaking equipment. The move aimed to keep China's advanced technology development in check. The H200 had been subject to the U.S. export ban, but the Donald Trump administration changed policy after last year's U.S.-China trade talks to allow sales to approved Chinese customers.
Separately, the Chinese government is maintaining its own import restrictions. If large volumes of U.S. chips flow in, domestic companies may keep choosing Nvidia products, which outperform Chinese-made offerings. That could clash with policy goals for Chinese chipmakers to expand their market and build technological capabilities.
It is in the same vein that China is not completely blocking U.S. chips. In AI model training, which is hard to replace immediately with Chinese products, U.S. chips are allowed on a limited basis, while in deploying AI models in actual services, the aim is to increase the use of Chinese chips.
Earlier, the information technology (IT) outlet The Information reported in July that authorities had notified Alibaba, ByteDance Ltd., and DeepSeek that they could allow limited purchases of H200s for AI model training. The Information said total approved volume could come in under 200,000 units. China is said to have required that domestic chips be used first for "inference," which deploys AI models in actual services.
AI model training is the process of processing vast amounts of data to improve a model's performance. Inference is the task of using a trained model to answer questions or generate outputs. The view is that by distinguishing training from inference to manage chip use, the Chinese government aims to secure the performance needed for AI development while growing the domestic chip market.
Semiconductor chips placed on a printed circuit board. The photo is unrelated to the article. /Courtesy of Reuters
◇ The paradox of technological self-reliance: burden in securing high-performance chips
The problem is that Chinese chips still do not fully match the performance of Nvidia's products. The H200 is not Nvidia's latest AI Semiconductor, but it is evaluated as offering performance that Chinese substitutes have not caught up to. It is especially useful for training large-scale AI models when combined with Nvidia's software.
As major Chinese tech companies such as Alibaba, ByteDance Ltd., and Tencent expand AI services, demand is also rising for high-performance chips like the H200. The drive by China's big tech firms to secure other U.S.-made chips is related to this demand.
Reuters reported last month that ByteDance Ltd., Alibaba, and Tencent ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards. The product is less powerful than the H200 but complies with U.S. export rules, and the list prices for the order volume total more than $35 billion (about 47 trillion won).
◇ Server asking prices surge in the gray market amid import limits
In particular, as U.S. export controls and China's import limits intersect, prices are surging in the unofficial chip market. According to Reuters, at the end of Oct., a server equipped with eight H200 chips in mainland China was offered for sale at more than 6 million yuan (about 1.2 billion won). That is about triple the price a year earlier. Servers equipped with Nvidia's next-generation Blackwell chips, which are subject to U.S. export controls, were reportedly offered at more than 20 million yuan (about 4 billion won) per unit.
Analysts say China's chip self-reliance policy could raise development costs for domestic AI companies in the short term. If imports are restricted when Chinese chips cannot fully replace Nvidia's products, securing high-performance chips could become even harder. Depending on whether the government approves large-scale imports in the future, Chinese AI companies' chip supply and development costs are also expected to be affected.

items.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
items.summary: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".
items.content:
Figure caption, Michel Barnier says there will be 'no cherry-picking' in a deal for the UK to returns to the EU
The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.
The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.
But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.
He said there was not a "single market Ã  la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.
Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.
But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.
He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms".
"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."
Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.
Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime .
Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.
Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.
Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.
He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.
Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.
The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".
Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."
Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [Â£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".
The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent Â£350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead".
Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly Â£350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS".
Critics have said that the Â£350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's Â£75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.
Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the Â£350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise.
âIn his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only Â£175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".
Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the Â£350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

items.title: Four things we learned this week about 2028 White House race
items.summary: The seismic Democratic gains in Congress could shape the presidential election, so who had a good night and who's making moves?
items.content:
Image caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD Vance
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro , swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.
California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.
Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio .
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz , who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis , who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
Former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie was blunt in his assessment: "The Trump era is over."
White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.
"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."
Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.
Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
Image caption, Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.
Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

items.content:
Anthropic IPO hits AI backlash after midterms show rebuke data centers
Anthropic's IPO could thrust the company into the spotlight at a moment when AI is very unpopular in the U.S.
In the midterm elections, voters opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases.
More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.
Anthropic’s breakneck rise: What to know before the IPO
Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.
The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.
From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.
Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases .
More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.
"People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public."
Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman . But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.
"Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more."
Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.
Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.
"I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public."
Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as US Speaker of the House Mike Johnson speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, DC, on Sept. 29, 2026.
AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion , "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.
In the risk factors section of its prospectus , Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.
Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.
"There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny."
Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over."
Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.
The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development.
"Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good."
